newsitem.title: USA: NYS comptroller raises questions about LIPA pact.
newsitem.headline: NYS comptroller raises questions about LIPA pact.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Tuesday raised a number of questions about a state authority's plans for the Long Island Lighting Company, which also were being probed at a state Assembly hearing.

"The persistent question in the ongong public debate over the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA) proposal is whether there is a better alternative," wrote H. Carl McCall, in a letter to the Authority's chairman, which he released.

LIPA Chairman Richard Kessel on Tuesday testified before the Assembly's energy committee. The Authority has said it hoped that the Public Authorities Control Board (PACB), which meets on Wednesday, would take up the plans, which call for LIPA to buy assets from LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which are merging. McCall wrote he would submit comments to the PACB, which has to approve all state and agency bond sales, before it makes its decision.

McCall cast doubts on whether LIPA's plan, which would be paid for with the nation's biggest-ever bond sale, would cut rates for Long Island residents, who now pay some of the highest electricty prices in the nation. "The dramatic, short-term reductions are inflated by over-borrowing and a debt structure that avoids payments in the early years." He called a three-year deferral of principal payments on the largest bond issue, and a five-year deferral of both principal and interest on a $462.5 million issue, bad public policy.

Some of the Authority's savings estimates also were attacked. "LIPA's savings projections are somewhat misleading because they are based on the assumption that LILCO rates would increase," McCall said, noting the company's rates now were frozen, and it was not clear increases would be approved, when a state regulator was forcing other utilities to restructure in order to cut costs and reduce rates.

The comptroller said ratepayers would best be served by promoting competition, saying it was problematic to set up a public utility just when deregulation and competition were breaking down utilities' monopolies. He also noted most of the push for competition was coming from Washington. "This raises the serious concern whether LIPA would remain economically sound in the future, when competition does arrive," he said.

Though he added full competition for Long Island's electricity business appeared to be many years away, he thought LIPA should speed its option to reduce how much power it buys from the new entity, which now starts in year seven.

While noting fund managers have said LIPA would be able to place its bonds, McCall feared other New York State issuers, including New York City, would be hurt, saying that in stable markets, the penalty could range from five to 15 basis points for two to four weeks before and after LIPA's proposed sales, which would total $7.6 billion. In a weak market, competing issuers might have to pay 10 to 25 basis points more in yield.

Finally, the state comptroller said that LILCO shareholders should not get a windfall, noting many utility investors have seen the changing industry environment hurt stock prices of other firms. "Fairness dictates that LILCO's shareholders should bear some of their company's liability."
